title: How to Spot and Avoid Stock Scams and Pump-and-Dump Schemes in Nigeria
summary: How pump-and-dump schemes and fake investment platforms work in Nigeria, the red flags to watch for, and how to protect yourself and verify operators.
body_markdown:
**In short:** A pump-and-dump scheme hypes a stock to inflate its price so those behind it can sell at the top, leaving latecomers with losses. Fake investment platforms and Ponzi schemes work similarly, promising guaranteed high returns. The biggest red flags are guaranteed returns, pressure to act fast, and unregistered operators. Always verify an operator’s SEC registration before investing. This is general information, not advice.


If you have spent any time in Nigerian investing groups on WhatsApp or Telegram, you have almost certainly seen it: a message urging you to buy a particular stock right now, before it “runs,” with promises of quick, easy profit. Sometimes it is a well-meaning but misguided tip. Sometimes it is a deliberate trap.


This guide explains how stock scams work, focusing on pump-and-dump schemes and the fake investment platforms that have flooded social media, so you can recognise them and protect your money. It is written to help you defend yourself, and it is general information, not investment advice. For the broader skill of judging a company on its merits, our[guide to choosing NGX stocks](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-choose-nigerian-stocks-a-beginners-guide/) is a useful companion, and our[complete guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) covers the basics.


## What is a pump-and-dump scheme?


A pump-and-dump scheme is a form of market manipulation where the price of a stock is artificially inflated through hype and false claims, so that those behind it can sell their shares at the peak before the price collapses.


The pattern is consistent. Those running the scheme take positions in a cheap, often thinly traded stock, one where a burst of buying can move the price sharply. They then “pump” it, flooding social media, group chats, and forums with excited claims that the stock is about to soar, sometimes with fabricated news or insider-sounding tips. As ordinary investors pile in and the price climbs, the organisers quietly “dump” their own shares at the inflated price. Once they stop buying and the hype fades, the price falls back, and the people who bought in late are left holding shares worth a fraction of what they paid.


Small, thinly traded stocks are the most common targets, because they are the easiest to move, but the tactic is not limited to them. The common thread is a sudden, hype-driven price surge that has nothing to do with the actual performance of the business underneath.


## How to recognise a pump-and-dump


The warning signs are usually visible if you know what to look for. A stock is being pushed hard on social media, WhatsApp, or Telegram, often by accounts you do not know. The messaging is urgent and emotional: buy now, this is about to explode, you will miss out. There is talk of a “sure” or “guaranteed” move. The stock itself is often small, obscure, or thinly traded, and the excitement is not backed by any real news about the company’s earnings or prospects. And the price may already have jumped sharply in a short time on no clear fundamental reason.


If you see a stock being aggressively hyped by strangers with promises of a quick, certain gain, treat that as a reason to stay away, not a reason to rush in. By the time a pump reaches you, an ordinary investor with no connection to the organisers, you are most likely the exit they are selling into.


## The bigger picture: fake platforms and Ponzi schemes


Beyond manipulating real stocks, a larger threat in Nigeria is the fake investment platform, and the regulator has sounded the alarm. In a public notice dated May 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission warned Nigerians about a surge of unregistered online investment schemes, many of which show the characteristics of Ponzi fraud. As[Punch reported](https://punchng.com/sec-warns-nigerians-against-fake-investment-schemes-on-social-media/) , these platforms promise unrealistic or guaranteed returns despite having no authorisation to operate in Nigeria’s capital market, and they spread aggressively across WhatsApp, Instagram, Telegram, Facebook, and TikTok.


A Ponzi scheme pays early investors with money from later ones rather than from any real profit, which is why it depends on constant recruitment and collapses when new money stops coming in. These schemes often dress themselves up in the language of stocks, forex, or crypto to sound legitimate, and they lean heavily on flashy marketing and testimonials. The SEC has been clear that only operators registered with it are legally permitted to provide investment and advisory services in Nigeria, and it regularly publishes notices naming specific unregistered operators it has flagged.


The practical takeaway is simple: a slick app or a busy group chat is not evidence of legitimacy. Registration with the regulator is.


## The universal red flags of any investment scam


Almost every investment scam, whether a pump-and-dump, a fake platform, or a Ponzi scheme, shares a recognisable set of warning signs. If you learn only one thing from this guide, learn these.


Guaranteed or unusually high returns are the single biggest red flag, because no legitimate investment can promise a guaranteed return, and the higher the promised return, the higher the risk or the more likely it is a fraud. Pressure and urgency are another, since scammers push you to act immediately so you do not have time to think or check. Any requirement to recruit other people to earn is a hallmark of a Ponzi structure. Unsolicited approaches, whether a direct message, a group-chat invitation, or an ad that adds you to an investment group, deserve deep suspicion. So do anonymous or unverifiable promoters, and accounts with little history or that impersonate well-known figures. And above all, if something sounds too good to be true, it almost always is.


None of these signs on its own proves fraud, but any of them should make you stop and verify before parting with a single naira.


## How to protect yourself


The good news is that protecting yourself comes down to a few reliable habits. The most important is to verify registration before you invest. Only SEC-registered operators are authorised to offer investment services in Nigeria, and you can check the registration status of any platform, company, or adviser through the[SEC](https://sec.gov.ng/) before committing funds. If an operator is not registered, that is your answer.


The rest follows from there. Use only regulated, SEC-registered platforms to invest. Bamboo, for example, is registered with the SEC, which means your investing happens within the regulated capital market rather than on an unaccountable app. Never make an investment decision based solely on a social media tip, a group chat, or an unsolicited message, no matter how confident or urgent it sounds. Do your own research on any company before you buy, judging it on its fundamentals rather than on hype. Be sceptical of guaranteed returns, because they do not exist in legitimate investing. And never let anyone rush you; a real opportunity will survive you taking a day to check it, while a scam depends on you not checking at all.


Investing through a properly regulated platform in genuinely listed companies is the opposite of a scam. You can invest in[Nigerian stocks](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) on Bamboo within that regulated framework.


## What to do if you suspect a scam


If you think you have encountered a scam, stop immediately and do not send any more money, even if you are told that paying a “fee” will release your funds, which is itself a common secondary scam. Gather what evidence you can, such as screenshots, account names, and transaction records. Report the scheme to the SEC, which maintains channels for reporting unregistered and fraudulent operators and can act on and publicise them. And warn others in your network, because these schemes spread through trust and word of mouth, and a single warning can stop someone else from losing money.


If you have already invested through a legitimate, regulated broker and simply made a poor stock choice, that is a different situation and an ordinary investing risk, not a scam. The distinction matters: scams involve deception and unregistered operators, while normal market losses are a risk that comes with legitimate investing.


## Frequently asked questions


**What is a pump-and-dump scheme?** It is a form of market manipulation where a stock’s price is inflated through hype and false claims so those behind it can sell at the top. When the hype fades, the price collapses, and investors who bought in late are left with heavy losses.


**How do I know if a stock tip is a scam?** Be suspicious of any tip that promises a guaranteed or quick gain, pressures you to buy immediately, comes from strangers or anonymous accounts, or pushes a small, obscure stock with no real news behind a sudden price jump. Legitimate investing does not work through urgent hype.


**How can I check if an investment platform is legitimate in Nigeria?** Verify its registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission before investing. Only SEC-registered operators are authorised to offer investment services in Nigeria. If a platform is not registered, do not invest.


**Why are guaranteed returns a red flag?** Because no legitimate investment can guarantee a return. All investing carries risk, and prices can fall as well as rise. A promise of guaranteed or unusually high returns is one of the clearest signs of a scam.


**What should I do if I have been scammed?** Stop sending money immediately, gather evidence such as screenshots and transaction records, report the scheme to the SEC, and warn others. Do not pay any further “fees” to release supposed funds, as that is a common follow-on scam.
